lesson.title: The Longest Day: Storming Fortress Europe
lesson.summary: On June 6, 1944, Allied forces launched the largest seaborne invasion in history on the beaches of Normandy, France, opening the long-awaited second front against Nazi Germany in Western Europe.
lesson.body:
Four years before D-Day, German blitzkrieg tactics had overrun France in a matter of weeks, using fast-moving tanks and coordinated air support to shatter Allied defenses and force France's surrender in June 1940. Reversing that outcome, driving the German army back out of Western Europe, required an invasion on a scale the world had never attempted before. After the United States entered the war and began building up forces and supplies in Britain, Soviet leader Joseph Stalin repeatedly pressed his allies to open a 'second front' in Western Europe to relieve pressure on Soviet forces, who were absorbing the brunt of the fighting against Germany in the east.

That second front arrived on June 6, 1944, a date remembered simply as D-Day. Under the command of General Dwight D. Eisenhower, the Supreme Allied Commander, more than 150,000 American, British, and Canadian troops crossed the English Channel and landed on five beaches along the coast of Normandy, France, codenamed Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword. The operation, known as Operation Overlord, had been planned for years and involved an enormous armada of ships and landing craft along with airborne troops, including the U.S. Army's 82nd and 101st Airborne Divisions, who parachuted behind enemy lines the night before to secure key roads and bridges.

The landings came at a heavy cost. American troops assaulting Omaha Beach faced some of the fiercest German resistance of the entire invasion, taking severe casualties as they crossed open beach under machine gun and artillery fire from fortified positions above. Despite the losses, Allied forces secured all five beachheads by the end of the day and began the difficult process of pushing inland through the hedgerow country of Normandy.

D-Day marked a turning point in the war in Europe. Within weeks, Allied forces broke out of Normandy, and by late August 1944 they had liberated Paris. With Soviet forces advancing from the east and Allied armies now pushing from the west, Germany faced a war on two major fronts in Europe that it could not sustain indefinitely, setting the stage for its eventual surrender less than a year later.
